name: Fondation Donwahi
overview: Contemporary art foundation in the Cocody district of Abidjan (AFP, 9 April 2013), at Boulevard des Martyrs (CAAC).
Official name Charles Donwahi Foundation for Contemporary Art, founded in 2008. Illa G. Donwahi is president and artistic director (CAAC; Mondriaan Fonds).

A group of art lovers, mostly African private-sector figures, set up the foundation, which opened in 2008. Over a little more than ten years Illa Donwahi turned her family home into its space (C&, Cédric Vincent, 18 December 2019).
funding_verdict: Fondation Donwahi: private: a group of mostly African private-sector founders, the family home as venue, with project partners

name: Kin ArtStudio
overview: Artist-run studio and residency in Kinshasa. The Pro Helvetia interview (12 November 2024) writes the name both as Kin ArtStudio and as KinArt Studios, and names Vitshois Mwilambwe Bondo as its founder.

Founded in 2011 by the visual artist Vitshois Mwilambwe Bondo (Art Africa magazine, 18 January 2017; Atelier Mondial). Bondo himself says Kinstudio began in 2010 as a project to support younger emerging artists, started as a master class in 2012, and found a physical space in 2011 (MOMAA interview, 1 March 2021).
Bondo describes it as a non-profit with a library and free internet access for research, and says he invites German artists to lead workshops (MOMAA).
funding_verdict: Kin ArtStudio: self-funded and sponsor-supported: the founder's art sales, plus sponsors and residency partners

name: Centro de Arte Contemporáneo de Quito
overview: Municipal contemporary art centre at Montevideo and Luis Dávila, in the Antiguo Hospital Militar, San Juan neighbourhood of Quito. Its guided tours end at the San Juan viewpoints (Expreso). The museum system's site calls it "el único espacio cultural especializado en arte contemporáneo en la ciudad y el país" (translation: the only cultural space specialised in contemporary art in the city and the country).

Part of the Sistema de Museos Quito, and one of five spaces run by the Fundación Museos de la Ciudad, with the Museo de la Ciudad, Museo del Carmen Alto, Museo Interactivo de Ciencia and Yaku Parque Museo del Agua.

Building: constructed between 1900 and 1913 as a military hospital (El Diario, July 2026). Expreso describes a heritage building of more than 6,000 square metres that has served as a sanatorium, military hospital, barracks and housing for several families. Its prison areas and the site of a former common grave are part of the tours.
funding_verdict: Centro de Arte Contemporáneo de Quito: run for the Municipality of Quito by the Fundación Museos de la Ciudad

name: Museo Nacional del Ecuador (MuNa)
overview: National museum of Ecuador, housed in the Casa de la Cultura Ecuatoriana building in Quito, on Avenida Patria between 6 de Diciembre and 12 de Octubre (Spanish Wikipedia).

Opened on 1 December 1969 as the Museo Arqueológico y Galerías de Arte Guillermo Pérez Chiriboga, founded by the Banco Central del Ecuador on the fifth and sixth floors of the bank's main building at La Alameda park (Spanish Wikipedia).
The government describes the planned new museum as housing 1.2 million cultural and heritage items from 12,000 years of history (Newsroom Infobae with EFE, 10 July 2026).
funding_verdict: Museo Nacional del Ecuador: run by the state ministry in charge of culture

name: Museo de Arte de El Salvador (MARTE)
overview: Private non-profit museum of Salvadoran art at Final Avenida de la Revolución, Colonia San Benito, San Salvador, beside the Monumento a la Revolución.

Opened to the public on 22 May 2003 (museum site). The Asociación Museo de Arte de El Salvador runs it, and English Wikipedia says the association was established in 2000. The museum says it has received more than 160,000 visitors since opening.
Designed by Salvadoran architect Salvador Choussy (born 1947) on a 6,520 m2 plot. English Wikipedia gives the construction cost as US$1.8 million.
funding_verdict: Museo de Arte de El Salvador (MARTE): private non-profit funded by contributions from individuals, companies and organisations, as the museum states

name: National Museum of Ethiopia
overview: Ethiopia's national museum in Addis Ababa, near the graduate school of Addis Ababa University.
It grew from the Institute of Archaeology, founded in 1958, and first showed finds from French-led excavations in northern Ethiopia (Wikipedia).
The artists Afewerk Tekle and Mamo Tessema helped found it, and Tessema served as curator.
funding_verdict: National Museum of Ethiopia: unconfirmed: government money is on record only for a replacement museum

press_items.title: Yemane Berhanu, "Finance Ministry Nods To Construction Of New National Museum" (2024)

name: Fiji Museum
overview: National museum of Fijian culture and history in Thurston Gardens, Cakobau Road, Suva (Fiji Museum).

The idea of a museum was first discussed in 1904, when Sir William Allardyce gave his collection to the Suva Town Board. The Fijian Society, formed in 1908, included a museum in its aims, and the collection stayed in the Town Hall until a fire in 1919 destroyed much of it (Fiji Museum).

Formally established in 1929 as "a Government Statutory Body with a Board of Trustees," governed by the Fiji Museum Act and the Preservation of Objects of Archaeological and Palaeontological Interest Act (Fiji Museum). Wikipedia says the Friends of Fiji Museum, a voluntary group, founded it in 1904.
funding_verdict: Fiji Museum: mainly public: Fiji government grants, with donor funding for digitisation from the US Embassy and the New Zealand High Commission

name: Oceania Centre for Arts, Culture and Pacific Studies (USP)
overview: Arts centre of the University of the South Pacific (USP) on its Laucala campus in Suva (USP page, archived September 2018).
Founded in 1997 as a special project of the USP University Council, with Professor Epeli Hau'ofa as its first director (USP page, archived 2018).
Originally the Oceania Centre for Arts and Culture. In 2008 Pacific Studies joined it, forming the present name (USP page, archived 2018).
funding_verdict: Oceania Centre for Arts, Culture and Pacific Studies: a unit of the University of the South Pacific, with Creative New Zealand and Creative Australia funding its 2026 residency

name: National Museum of Finland
overview: Finland's national museum of cultural history, at Mannerheimintie 34 in the Töölö district of Helsinki.
Its collections began at the Royal Academy of Turku in the eighteenth century and passed to state administration in 1893 (stated by the space).

Herman Gesellius, Armas Lindgren and Eliel Saarinen won the 1902 competition for the building, construction began in 1905, the exhibitions opened in January 1916 and the institution took its present name that year.
funding_verdict: National Museum of Finland: public: the Finnish state through the Finnish Heritage Agency
wider_context: On 24 October 2024 the Finnish Heritage Agency ended staff negotiations aimed at cutting EUR 3.2 million from its 2025 operating costs: about 150 of roughly 220 permanent employees were to be laid off temporarily, and the agency announced reduced services and museum closures.
The agency said the National Museum earns no income during construction and that a late opening would cost more than EUR 250,000 a month.

name: Siida Sámi Museum (Saamelaismuseo Siida)
overview: National museum of Sámi culture and regional museum for cultural environment tasks in the Sámi area, at Inarintie 46, Inari, Finnish Lapland, with an open-air museum of about 50 historic buildings (siida.fi, museot.fi).

Founded in 1959 by the Sámi association Sámi Litto as the Sámi Museum, with the first open-air museum buildings moved to the site in 1960. It opened to the public in summer 1963 as the first independent Sámi museum in the Nordic countries (siida.fi).

The Sámi Museum Foundation, established in 1986, owns the collections and the open-air museums and runs the museum. Its board has eight members elected for four-year terms, and at least four must be Sámi-born citizens of Finland (siida.fi).
funding_verdict: Siida Sámi Museum: mainly public: Finnish ministry money, with Finnish foundations for the exhibition renewal

name: Serlachius Museums
overview: Art museum in Mänttä, Finland, on two sites: Serlachius Manor (Kartano, Joenniementie 47) and Serlachius Pääkonttori (R. Erik Serlachiuksen katu 2) in central Mänttä, the former G. A. Serlachius headquarters (Serlachius).

The paper mill owners began collecting art more than a hundred years ago. The collection holds about 10,000 works (Serlachius). It centres on Finland's Golden Age art, with old European art, older Finnish art, early modernist works and a growing body of contemporary art (foundation page).

The Gösta Serlachius Fine Arts Foundation, established in 1933 to preserve and build Gösta Serlachius's art collection and "beautifying Mänttä with art", maintains the museum complex and the Serlachius Residency (foundation page).
funding_verdict: Serlachius Museums: foundation-run: the Gösta Serlachius Fine Arts Foundation, established in 1933 to preserve and build Gösta Serlachius's art collection

name: Frac des Pays de la Loire
overview: Regional contemporary art fund (Fonds régional d'art contemporain) based at La Fleuriaye in Carquefou, northeast of Nantes, with a collection of more than 2,000 works (Frac website, French Wikipedia).

Created in 1982 as part of the national Frac network, a partnership between the French State and the regions (Frac website). Its first home was the Abbaye royale de Fontevraud, then the Garenne-Lemot villa in Clisson from 1988 and a converted warehouse in Nantes in 1994 (Frac website).
The Carquefou building opened in 2000 as the first Frac building designed for the purpose, by the architect Jean-Claude Pondevie (Frac website).
funding_verdict: Frac des Pays de la Loire: funded by the State and the Pays de la Loire Region, with Sodebo as main patron

name: 49 Nord 6 Est – Frac Lorraine
overview: Regional public collection of contemporary art for the Lorraine part of the Grand Est region, with a free exhibition space in the historic centre of Metz at 1 bis rue des Trinitaires. Its formal name is Fonds régional d'art contemporain de Lorraine.
Founded in 1984 as a "nomad contemporary art fund" (Wikipedia), part of the national Frac programme started in 1982 on the principle of shared financing between the state and the regional councils.
Named "49 Nord 6 Est" for the geodesic position of its building (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: 49 Nord 6 Est Frac Lorraine: mainly public: Région Grand Est and the French state

name: Le 19, Crac
overview: Regional centre for contemporary art at 19 avenue des Alliés, opposite Montbéliard Ville railway station and 15 minutes from the Belfort-Montbéliard TGV station (le19crac.com; DCA).

Founded in 1993 and opened in 1995; since 24 December 2018 it holds the national label Centre d'art contemporain d'intérêt national (le19crac.com; Montbéliard council deliberation of 18 December 2023).
It is an association under the French law of 1901, chaired by Liliane Dangel (2024 to 2027 objectives agreement and its 2025 amendment).
funding_verdict: Le 19, Crac: public: the State (DRAC Bourgogne-Franche-Comté), the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté Region, the City of Montbéliard and Pays de Montbéliard Agglomération

name: Cité internationale des arts
overview: Artist residence in Paris with 310 live-in studios on two sites: the Marais, at 18 rue de l'Hôtel de Ville, about 280 artists at a time, and Montmartre, at 24 rue Norvins, around thirty studios (stated by the Cité).

Officially inaugurated on 20 May 1965 in the Marais. The idea dates to 1937, when the architect Félix Brunau and the Finnish artist Eero Snellman proposed it. The Montmartre site opened in 1971 (stated by the Cité).
A nonprofit private foundation recognised as a public-benefit body under French law, by decree of 14 September 1957 (stated by the Cité).
funding_verdict: Cité internationale des arts: partner-funded: a cooperative model of public and private residency partners

press_items.title: La rédaction, "Remous à la Cité internationale des arts" (23 February 2007)

name: CEAAC
overview: Contemporary art centre at 7 rue de l'Abreuvoir, Strasbourg, run as an association under the local law of 1908. The Ministry of Culture announced on 1 July 2024 that it awarded the centre the label "centre d'art contemporain d'intérêt national" and names Alice Motard as its director.
Has worked from its current building since 1995. The centre says it played a driving role in placing artworks in Alsace's public space in its early years.

The building is the former Neunreiter store: Eugène Neunreiter, founder in 1865 of the glassware and porcelain firm of that name, bought the property in 1878 and set up a sales shop, warehouses and housing. Ferdinand Kalweit was the architect and Adolf Zilly the painter. Main building campaigns date from 1898 and 1902, with an extension in 1923 (Mérimée notice).
funding_verdict: CEAAC: four named public funders and one private patron: the State (DRAC Grand Est), Région Grand Est, Collectivité européenne d'Alsace and the City of Strasbourg; SAS Neunreiter

name: Crac Occitanie
overview: Regional contemporary art centre on the Canal Royal in Sète, facing the port and the Mediterranean (Crac Occitanie).

Opened in 1997, managed by the Occitanie region. Noëlle Tissier directed it from 1997 to 2017 and Marie Cozette has directed it since 2018 (Crac Occitanie). French Wikipedia says Cozette was appointed by Carole Delga, president of the Regional Council.

Building: a former refrigerated warehouse for fish preservation, renovated in 1997 by the architect Lorenzo Piqueras, with about 1,200 square metres of exhibition space over two levels (Crac Occitanie). French Wikipedia says the conversion ran from 1995 to 1997.
funding_verdict: Crac Occitanie: managed by the Région Occitanie, with State support

name: Musée de Tahiti et des Îles – Te Fare Iamanaha
overview: Museum of the natural and cultural heritage of Oceania, especially Polynesia, at Nu'uroa point in Punaauia, in a park of about three hectares with an ethnobotanical garden (museum website).
French Wikipedia puts it about 15 km southwest of Papeete, on a plot facing the Tahiti lagoon.

A museum created in Papeete in 1917 by the Société des Études océaniennes was merged into it. The government bought the site in 1967, the Territorial Assembly voted the creation in 1974, and the museum opened in the 1970s. French Wikipedia gives 30 May 1977 for the inauguration.
funding_verdict: Musée de Tahiti et des Îles: mainly public: the government of French Polynesia, with State and Pays money for the renovation

name: Kropka (Belarusian community space; listed in place of 'Krokva')
overview: Belarusian community centre in a two-room apartment with a courtyard in a residential building in Tbilisi's Sololaki neighbourhood (Transitions, Tanya Hendzel, "A Belarusian Island in the Caucasus", 22 July 2024).
Opened in March 2022 as a coworking space, conceived by Belarusian activists who fled repression in Belarus. It soon grew into meetings and events (Transitions). "Kropka" means "Point" (Transitions).
Day-to-day operations were run by a volunteer, Olga. Viktoria handled administration and was paid by donor organisations (names are pseudonyms in the article) (Transitions).
funding_verdict: Kropka: donor-funded: international foundation grants and visitor donations
wider_context: Pozirk: Georgia's "foreign influence" law was inspired by a Russian law that the Kremlin uses to persecute opponents; Pozirk also writes that Georgian authorities recently rejected several Belarusians' asylum applications and that activists and journalists are often barred from re-entering the country.
Wikipedia names the law the "Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence" and gives 14 May 2024 as the date of its third reading in parliament, passed 84 votes to 30.

Pozirk lists the law among the reasons for Kropka's closing, and Transitions says Kropka, which relies on international foundation grants, avoids Georgian authorities since the "foreign agent law" was adopted.

name: Tbilisi Photography & Multimedia Museum (TPMM)
overview: Non-governmental, not-for-profit museum dedicated to the contemporary image, at 14 M. Kostava Street, Tbilisi. It calls itself the first institution in Georgia of that kind (stated by the space).

Nestan Nijaradze co-founded the non-profit in 2017 with a group of women professionals (Freunde von Freunden, Ann-Christin Schubert, undated). It opened in 2019 (Equal Times, Clément Girardot, 24 October 2024).

Housed at Stamba, a former Soviet-era publishing house that became a boutique hotel in 2018 (stated by the space). Freunde von Freunden describes a 950 square metre industrial-style exhibition space that grew out of the Tbilisi Photo Festival.
funding_verdict: TPMM: donor-funded non-profit: Swiss development agency, with space provided by Adjara Group
wider_context: Georgia's Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence passed its third reading on 14 May 2024, and parliament overrode the president's veto on 28 May 2024; it requires civil society and media organisations that receive more than 20 per cent of their annual revenue from abroad to register as "implementing organisations of foreign power interests" (ECNL, 24 May 2024).

Equal Times (Clément Girardot, 24 October 2024) says the government introduced the measure, which it calls a law requiring NGOs to declare themselves "foreign agents" if they receive funding from outside Georgia, after several weeks of mass protests, and that it was inspired by a similar Russian law.

Nijaradze told Equal Times the law "has created administrative difficulties" for the museum and that it set up a new NGO in Lithuania "in a more secure legal environment". She said she fears "a return to censorship", linked in the article to a 17 September law banning "LGBT propaganda".
